implementation_notes: Foundation's NSLock exposes lock()/unlock(); the scope-bound release is written as `lock.lock(); defer { lock.unlock() }`, and defer runs on every exit path including thrown errors, so the pairing survives error handling and early returns. NSLock is non-recursive and must be unlocked by the thread that locked it; NSRecursiveLock exists for genuinely re-entrant code but usually signals a design problem. For new code on current deployment targets Synchronization.Mutex is the better choice, and actor isolation removes the lock entirely when the state can live on an actor.
pitfalls: A defer registered before lock() runs even if acquisition never happened; register it immediately after a successful lock and keep the pair adjacent.
Unlocking from a different thread (after a continuation or thread hop) is undefined behaviour; lock and unlock must stay on the same thread.
NSLock is not recursive - locking twice on one thread deadlocks permanently.
Swift 6 strict concurrency will reject class state shared across concurrency domains unless it is Sendable or actor-isolated; raw locks alone do not satisfy the compiler.

variants.name: Synchronization.Mutex.withLock (Swift 6)
variants.implementation_notes: Swift 6 adds the Synchronization module: Mutex<Value> owns the value it protects and offers withLock, which acquires, runs the body and releases on every path - no manual unlock and no defer, closer to Rust's Mutex than to NSLock. Prefer it for new code where the deployment target allows (iOS 18 / macOS 15 or later); NSLock remains correct on older targets, and actors are the alternative when the state can be isolated rather than locked.
pitfalls: Availability is gated to iOS 18 / macOS 15 and later; older targets need NSLock or an actor.
Mutex is non-recursive: re-entering withLock deadlocks.
The withLock body is non-escaping - an escaping closure that captures the protected value moves the access outside the lock (the compiler rejects most of these, but not all through indirection).
Mutex is ~Copyable, so it cannot be copied into a closure or stored carelessly; keep it as a stored property.
